precepts.text: And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ. The seventh trump brings forth completion, the same way the seventh circuit brought down Jericho.
precepts.point: On the seventh day, because of their faith, the Most High brought down the walls of Jericho flat. Nothing is accidental with the Most High: the seventh day rest, Naaman dipped seven times, Jericho compassed seven times by seven priests with seven trumpets.

note.label: 70 Times 7: The Perfection of Mercy Through Christ

precepts.why:
At Jericho it was sevens all the way through: “seven priests shall bear before the ark seven trumpets of rams’ horns: and the seventh day ye shall compass the city seven times, and the priests shall blow with the trumpets.” Six days they went round once, and on the seventh day, the Sabbath day, seven times. “And it came to pass at the seventh time, when the priests blew with the trumpets, Joshua said unto the people, Shout; for the Lord hath given you the city.” Because of their faith, on the seventh day the Most High brought the walls down flat.

Revelation shows the same pattern at the end: “And the seventh angel sounded; and there were great voices in heaven, saying, The kingdoms of this world are become the kingdoms of our Lord, and of his Christ; and he shall reign for ever and ever.” The seventh angel sounded the trump, and that brought forth completion. It is the same thing that happened when our forefathers walked around the walls of Jericho.

Seven represents completion and totality, and it also represents complete deliverance. Nothing is accidental with the Most High; he uses seven as a form of deliverance. From the beginning it has been there: the seventh day rest, Naaman dipped seven times, and Jericho compassed seven times by seven priests with seven trumpets.

So the seventh trumpet at Jericho gave Israel the city, and the seventh trumpet in Revelation gives the kingdoms of this world to our Lord and his Christ. All of this is a representation of Christ, and it points to the complete deliverance of Israel when he reigns.

precepts.text: Keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make the camp of Israel a curse and trouble it.
precepts.point: Because of that trespass Israel could not stand before their enemies but turned their backs, for they were accursed; the Lord would not be with them any more except they destroyed the accursed from among them, and Achan and his family and all that belonged to him were destroyed and burned, and a heap set upon them, because he broke the covenant.

note.label: Deuteronomy 23: Who May Enter the Congregation and the Holy Camp

precepts.why:
“When the host goeth forth against thine enemies, then keep thee from every wicked thing.” When Israel went to war, they were to keep themselves from every wicked thing, and the example is Achan.

Before Jericho fell, Israel was warned: “And ye, in any wise keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed, when ye take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of Israel a curse, and trouble it.” That is this law spoken to the host going forth: one wicked thing taken makes the whole camp of Israel a curse and troubles it.

precepts.text: If ye go to war against the enemy that oppresseth you, blow an alarm with the trumpets, and ye shall be remembered before the Lord and saved from your enemies.
precepts.point: This is the spirit behind the men of Israel rehearsing the righteous acts with trumpets and shofars today, at the camps and at the new moons; it is spiritual and an act of faith.

note.label: Joshua 6: The Fall of Jericho and the Faith of Rahab

precepts.why:
The battle plan came from the Lord: seven priests bearing seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark, and at the long blast the great shout, and the wall falls down flat. The trumpets were commanded for war: “And if ye go to war in your land against the enemy that oppresseth you, then ye shall blow an alarm with the trumpets; and ye shall be remembered before the Lord your God, and ye shall be saved from your enemies.”

The blowing of the trumpets activates the armies of the Lord, the angels, to help in battle. Remember Elisha's servant: when his eyes were opened he saw the host of angels that were there warring and protecting Israel. Blow the alarm, be remembered before the Lord, and be saved from your enemies; that is what happened at Jericho.

This is the spirit behind the men of Israel rehearsing the righteous acts with trumpets and shofars today, at the camps and at the new moons; it is spiritual and an act of faith.

precepts.text: By works a man is justified, and not by faith only; Rahab the harlot was justified by works; faith without works is dead.
precepts.point: All the silver and gold and vessels of brass and iron were consecrated unto the Lord, separated and sanctified for his treasury alone: nobody was to gain personally from this war.

note.label: Joshua 6: The Fall of Jericho and the Faith of Rahab

precepts.why:
“only Rahab the harlot shall live, she and all that are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent.” She made a covenant with the spies: she would conceal them and assist Israel, knowing the Lord was with Israel, as long as her family was saved when the city fell. Rahab was a Canaanite, a heathen, yet the heathen can be blessed when they do it to benefit Israel; blessed is he that blesseth thee.

Rahab is the scripture's own example that a man is justified by works and not by faith only. “Ye see then how that by works a man is justified, and not by faith only. Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way? For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also.”

Faith and works go hand in hand, for your actions prove whether you believe. Rahab did not only believe the Lord was with Israel; she received the messengers and sent them out another way, and that is why she lived.

precepts.text: Set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments; works means keeping the commandments.
precepts.point: All the silver and gold and vessels of brass and iron were consecrated unto the Lord, separated and sanctified for his treasury alone: nobody was to gain personally from this war.

note.label: Joshua 6: The Fall of Jericho and the Faith of Rahab

precepts.why:
Works by the Bible's own dictionary is keeping his commandments: “That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments”. Set your hope in God, forget not his works, but keep his commandments.

So when James says Rahab was justified by works, that is what works means. Faith without works is dead, and works is keeping the commandments. Rahab's faith showed in what she did.

precepts.text: The Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.
precepts.point: All the silver and gold and vessels of brass and iron were consecrated unto the Lord, separated and sanctified for his treasury alone: nobody was to gain personally from this war.

note.label: Joshua 6: The Fall of Jericho and the Faith of Rahab

precepts.why:
“Talk no more so exceeding proudly; let not arrogancy come out of your mouth: for the Lord is a God of knowledge, and by him actions are weighed.” Words say a lot, but actions always speak louder, and by him actions are weighed.

Rahab's actions were weighed and she lived. And the warning cuts the other way: keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest ye make yourselves accursed and make the camp of Israel a curse, and trouble it. Your individual sins affect the whole nation of Israel, your brothers, your sisters, and the children. That is why we must examine ourselves whether we be in the faith. The silver, gold, and vessels of brass and iron were consecrated unto the Lord, separated and sanctified for his treasury alone: nobody was to gain personally from this war.

precepts.text: Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet; the spirit of the great shout at the wall.
precepts.point: The people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city and utterly destroyed all that was in it, both man and woman, young and old, ox, sheep, and ass, with the edge of the sword.

note.label: Joshua 6: The Fall of Jericho and the Faith of Rahab

precepts.why:
“So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat”. That shout is Isaiah 58:1 in action: “Cry aloud, spare not, lift up thy voice like a trumpet, and shew my people their transgression, and the house of Jacob their sins.”

The sound coming out of their mouths with the trumpets broke everything down, like thousands of lions roaring at once. Lift up thy voice like a trumpet: that is the spirit of the great shout at the wall, and the wall came down flat so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and took it.

precepts.text: Rahab the harlot and her father's household were saved alive and she dwelt in Israel, because she knew the fame of what the God of Israel had done and that the hearts of her people had melted; she knew the Most High was the true living God.
precepts.point: Does that mean she would inherit the kingdom as a Moabitess? No. She joined herself under Israel and acknowledged her place in the hierarchy under Israel, and the scriptures give examples of strangers who did the same.

note.label: Ruth 1: Naomi and Ruth Return from Moab

precepts.why:
Rahab is another stranger who joined herself under Israel. “And Joshua saved Rahab the harlot alive, and her father’s household, and all that she had; and she dwelleth in Israel even unto this day; because she hid the messengers, which Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.”

Rahab knew the fame of what the God of Israel had done and that the hearts of her people had melted; she knew the Most High was the true living God. So she and her father's household were saved alive, and she dwelt in Israel. Like Ruth saying thy God my God, she acknowledged Israel's God and took her place under Israel.

precepts.text: Joshua's curse: whoever rebuilds Jericho lays its foundation in his firstborn and sets its gates in his youngest son.
precepts.point: In his days Hiel of Bethel rebuilds Jericho, laying its foundation in his firstborn Abiram and setting up its gates in his youngest Segub, according to the word spoken by Joshua.

note.label: 1 Kings 16: Baasha to Ahab and the Rise of Baal Worship

precepts.why:
When Jericho fell, Joshua laid a curse on it: “Cursed be the man before the Lord, that riseth up and buildeth this city Jericho: he shall lay the foundation thereof in his firstborn, and in his youngest son shall he set up the gates of it.”

In Ahab’s days it came to pass word for word. Hiel the Beth–elite built Jericho, and “laid the foundation thereof in Abiram his firstborn, and set up the gates thereof in his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the Lord, which he spake by Joshua the son of Nun.” The word of the Most High by Joshua stood, generations later.
